title: Highest-Protein Foods: A Practical Ranking per 100 Grams

seo.title: Highest-Protein Foods per 100 Grams
seo.meta_description: Compare high-protein foods per 100 grams and by realistic serving, including cooked vs dry foods and protein per calorie.
seo.search_intent: Compare protein-rich foods and understand how cooking, water and serving size change the numbers.

excerpt: Aged cheeses, seeds and lean cooked meats rank among the most protein-dense foods per 100 grams, but serving size and water content can change which foods contribute the most protein to an actual meal.
content_html:
Chicken, eggs and tuna are familiar high-protein foods, but a strict per-100-gram comparison puts some aged cheeses and seeds even higher. That does not automatically make them better protein choices. A 1-ounce serving of Parmesan and a 5-ounce chicken breast play very different roles in a meal.

Protein ranking per 100 grams

FoodApprox. protein
Parmesan cheese35.8 g
Hulled hemp seeds31.6 g
Cooked chicken breast31.0 g
Pumpkin seeds30.2 g
Cooked turkey breast29.5 g
Cooked yellowfin tuna29.2 g
Lean cooked beef~28 g
Lean cooked pork loin~27 g
Peanuts25.8 g
Drained canned sardines24.6 g
Cooked salmon22.1 g
Almonds21.2 g
Tempeh~20 g
Cooked soybeans18.2 g
Whole egg~12.6 g
Cooked lentils9.0 g

Variety, cut, brand and preparation change the exact values. What matters most is comparing foods in a recognizable state and not treating dry and cooked foods as if their water content were the same.

Why dry foods often rank so high

Water takes up much of a food's weight. Parmesan contains far less water than cottage cheese, and seeds contain far less than cooked beans. With less water, protein, fat and minerals become more concentrated per 100 grams.

Parmesan is about 35.8 g protein per 100 g, while cottage cheese is commonly around 11–13 g. Yet a typical Parmesan serving may be 1 ounce, while a cottage-cheese serving can be a half cup or more.

Dry vs cooked lentils

Dry lentils provide about 24.6 g protein per 100 g. Cooked lentils provide about 9.0 g per 100 g. The main reason is water absorption, not destruction of two-thirds of the protein.

LentilsProtein/100 gApprox. water
Dry24.6 g8 g
Cooked9.0 g70 g

The reverse happens with meat. Raw chicken breast may contain roughly 22–23 g protein per 100 g, while cooked breast is closer to 31 g because cooking drives off water and concentrates the remaining solids.

Animal foods with the most concentrated protein

Lean cooked meat and fish are consistently high. Cooked chicken breast is about 31 g/100 g, yellowfin tuna about 29.2 g and cooked salmon about 22.1 g. Aged cheeses can be even higher by weight because they are drier, but they also concentrate fat, calories and sodium.

Plant foods that stand out

Hemp and pumpkin seeds are around 31.6 and 30.2 g/100 g. Peanuts provide about 25.8 g, almonds 21.2 g and tempeh about 20 g. For a main meal, soy foods and legumes are often easier to eat in protein-significant portions than seeds.

Serving size changes the picture

FoodTypical example servingApprox. protein
Cooked chicken breast5 oz / 142 g44 g
Cooked turkey breast5 oz / 142 g42 g
Cooked tuna5 oz / 142 g41 g
Tempeh5 oz / 142 g~28 g
Cooked lentils1 cup / ~200 g18 g
Parmesan1 oz / 28 g10 g
Hemp seeds1 oz / 28 g9 g
Almonds1 oz / 28 g6 g

A food can lead the per-100-gram ranking and still contribute less protein to a meal because the usual serving is much smaller.

Protein per calorie is another question

Seeds, nuts and aged cheese are protein-rich but calorie-dense. Cooked cod provides about 22.8 g protein for roughly 105 calories per 100 g; almonds provide about 21.2 g protein for roughly 579 calories. The almonds also bring fiber, vitamin E, magnesium and unsaturated fat, so protein efficiency is not a complete measure of nutritional quality.

How much protein do adults need?

The U.S. Daily Value for protein is 50 g on a 2,000-calorie diet, while individual needs vary with body size, age, activity and other factors. The Recommended Dietary Allowance for most adults is 0.8 g per kilogram of body weight per day, equivalent to about 56 g for a 154-pound / 70-kg adult.

The useful takeaway

Protein concentration, serving size and total food quality answer different questions. Chicken, fish, dairy, eggs, soy foods, legumes, nuts and seeds can all make meaningful contributions. The most useful comparison is the one that matches how the food is actually eaten.

Sources

Food composition values come from USDA FoodData Central. U.S. protein reference values are summarized by the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements and FDA labeling guidance.

faq.question: Which food has the most protein per 100 grams?
faq.answer: Among common foods, aged cheeses and some seeds rank very high. Parmesan is about 35.8 g/100 g and hulled hemp seeds about 31.6 g/100 g.

faq.question: Does chicken have more protein than lentils?
faq.answer: Cooked chicken breast is about 31 g/100 g versus about 9 g for cooked lentils. Dry lentils are about 24.6 g/100 g before they absorb water.

faq.question: Why does cooked meat show more protein per 100 g?
faq.answer: Cooking removes water, so the same protein is concentrated into less weight.
